They’d be eliminated from NBA Cup play with a loss, according to the NBA’s rundown of all potential Cup group scenarios.

stories.title: LeBron Log No. 6: A Rocky night, a shooting lesson and a fight over ‘Bron'
stories.summary: James took the Sixers to see "I Play Rocky," knocked down threes against Portland and sued the makers of a betting research app.
stories.detailText: LeBron Log No. 6: A Rocky night, a shooting lesson and a fight over ‘Bron' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia It was another eventful week for LeBron James. When is it not? That’s why we started the LeBron Log in the first place. The King spent his latest week taking his teammates to the movies, fighting over his name in federal court and producing his best three-point shooting performance as a Sixer days after recording a podcast about the craft. This week also marks 20 years since James faced the Sixers alongside Allen Iverson. Welcome to the sixth edition. WE WATCH ROCKY James found an appropriate choice for the Sixers’ latest team outing. He organized a private screening of I Play Rocky on Friday night for players, their families and members of the basketball operations staff. The film follows Sylvester Stallone’s fight to get the original Rocky made while insisting that he play the title character. “I mean, it’s Rocky. We in Philly,” James said. “I heard it was a great movie, and we had a night off. I’ve got a few connections, and I was able to bring that to my teammates and this organization for us to watch it. I thought it was a great movie. Unbelievably cast. Everyone looked like exactly who they were portraying. That is Hollywood for you. It was pretty cool.” The Sixers shared photos of James alongside Jaylen Brown, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, Labaron Philon Jr., Jabari Walker, Tacko Fall and Adem Bona. “Movie night, courtesy of LeBron,” the team wrote. View this post on Instagram The nationwide release of I Play Rocky came less than two weeks before Philadelphia celebrates the 50th anniversary of the original film on Dec. 3. Nick Nurse could not attend because of a previous commitment, but he received positive reviews from his players. “They went, they said it was very good, they loved it,” Nurse said. “The big takeaway was how much Anthony actually looked like Rocky. Or Sylvester Stallone. One in the same.” James’ first season in Philadelphia now includes a private Rocky screening. A trip up the Art Museum steps remains available for a future edition. FROM THE PODCAST TO THE BUZZER James and Steve Nash devoted the latest episode of their Mind the Game podcast to the art of shooting. The two examined shooting form, confidence, repetitions, free throws and some of their favorite jumpers. James also revealed one detail that can affect what he does after catching the ball. “I’m a guy who don’t like shooting against the laces,” James said. “So sometimes I’ll come up on a quick stop and I’m about to raise and I can feel the laces not fixed. I’ll turn that into a pump fake.” The episode was released Nov. 17, while James was experiencing an extended struggle from three-point range. It did not provide an instant fix. James went 1 for 5 from three against Orlando and missed his lone attempt against Milwaukee. He entered Monday night’s meeting with Portland shooting 21.7 percent from deep through his first 13 games. Then he caught fire. James made all three of his first-half attempts from three. He ended the second quarter by pump-faking, stepping to his left and beating the buzzer with a corner three that tied the game at 69. Nobody could see where the laces sat on the catch. The pump fake was clear. James finished 4 for 5 from three and scored a season-high 23 points on 8-for-13 shooting. It was his third consecutive game with at least 20 points, following 22 against Orlando and 21 against Milwaukee. The Sixers lost to Portland, 128-111, but James produced his best long-range performance since joining them. Six days after discussing the art of shooting, he provided a brief demonstration. A FIGHT OVER ‘BRON’ James is also attempting to protect one of his most recognizable nicknames. James and LBJ Trademarks LLC filed a federal lawsuit on Nov. 17 against PlayVision Inc. and its founders over a sports-betting research app initially called “Bron.” The complaint alleges that the company used an AI-generated version of James in an advertisement without his permission. The figure wore a No. 23 jersey with “Bron” across the back and resembled James through its voice, build and tattoos. It also scrolled through wagers involving NBA players. The lawsuit alleges that the advertisement falsely created the impression that James endorsed the app and suggested that he considered betting on NBA games. The complaint said the video received roughly 1 million views before it was removed. “The integrity of NBA competition, and the public’s confidence that players are not betting on the games they play, is of paramount importance to the league, its players and its fans,” the complaint said. “Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views.” The app offered odds comparisons, betting trends and tracking tools but did not directly accept wagers, according to its developer. PlayVision renamed it “Evie” on Nov. 18, one day after James filed the lawsuit. James is seeking an injunction and unspecified damages. The case remains active in the Southern District of New York. CLEVELAND – NOVEMBER 25: LeBron James #23 of the Cleveland Cavaliers looks to pass off when double teamed by the Philadelphia 76ers November 25, 2006 at The Quicken Loans Arena in Cleveland, Ohio. Copyright 2006 NBAE (Photo by David Liam Kyle/NBAE via Getty Images) TWENTY YEARS LATER James spent Thanksgiving weekend in 2006 on the other side of the Sixers-Cavaliers matchup. On Nov. 25, 2006, a 21-year-old James recorded 25 points, 11 assists, four rebounds and one block in Cleveland’s 108-95 win over Philadelphia. Donning the Cavs’ old-school orange threads, he played nearly 41 minutes. Iverson led the Sixers with 31 points. Andre Iguodala added 17 points and eight rebounds, while Kyle Korver made three three-pointers off the bench. James recorded 11 assists that night. Nearly 20 years later, another 11-assist performance against Indiana moved him past Jason Kidd for third place in NBA history. The 2006 meeting also came near the end of Iverson’s original run with Philadelphia. The Sixers traded him to Denver less than a month later. James was 21. Iverson was nearing his departure. Twenty years later, James is wearing a Sixers uniform and Iverson’s No. 3 hangs above his home floor.

stories.title: Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double
stories.summary: The Sixers improved to 3-0 Saturday night by beating the Bucks at Xfinity Mobile Arena.
stories.detailText: Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season. Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists. On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards. The Sixers’ absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team’s matchup with the Pistons on Sunday. Here are observations on the Sixers’ victory Saturday: Wade debuts, Embiid starts in style Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James’ place. He’d missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain. The 3-and-D forward scored the night’s first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession. Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team’s offense in the early going. The Sixers’ seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man. Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead. One of Embiid’s assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter. Second-quarter struggles The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn’t enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter. Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run. Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn’t carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly. Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins’ three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead. The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they’d fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win. The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team’s transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game’s first 19 fast-break points. Star trio produces The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup. Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup. Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks’ odds of a road win. They’d all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter. Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers’ lead to 97-87. The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel’el Ware’s put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee’s deficit to 117-114. The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure. For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

stories.title: Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers
stories.summary: The Sixers’ five-game winning streak was snapped by the Trail Blazers.
stories.detailText: Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia The Sixers’ five-game winning streak was snapped Monday night by the Trail Blazers. With a 128-111 defeat at Xfinity Mobile Arena, the Sixers dropped their first game of the year against Western Conference opposition and fell to 14-4. Portland improved to 11-6. LeBron James had a season-high 23 points and six rebounds. Tyrese Maxey scored 22 points and Jaylen Brown added 20. Deni Avdija led the Blazers with 31 points and seven assists. Donovan Clingan posted 15 points and 18 rebounds. The Sixers were missing Joel Embiid (illness). Ja Morant (left hamstring strain) and Shaedon Sharpe (right knee meniscus surgery) were among Portland’s sidelined players. Next on the Sixers’ schedule is a Wednesday night game vs. the Heat. Here are observations on their blowout loss to the Blazers: Walker starts, Brown back in lineup Jabari Walker, listed at 6-foot-7, defied conventional wisdom by winning the opening tip-off against the 7-2 Cllingan. Maxey then canned a three-pointer. Brown scored the Sixers’ next four points with a pair of free throws and a short jumper. VJ Edgecombe’s layup gave the team a 9-2 lead. Brown and Dean Wade both returned Monday after sitting out the last two games with left hamstring injuries. Avdija got hot in the first quarter. He scored 11 quick points, made his first four field goals and helped the Blazers avoid a serious early deficit. The Sixers took a 32-30 edge with 9.3 seconds left in the first when Walker jammed in a put-back dunk. The former Portland second-round draft pick played 17 minutes in his second start of the season and continued to look deserving of a rotation spot. He posted 10 points and five rebounds. Nurse tries different center options Adem Bona was available again following an eight-game absence with a cervical spine sprain. However, Dominick Barlow checked in first to back up Walker. Barlow had an outstanding start to his night. He scored a clever lefty push shot over Clingan and threw down a dunk in the first quarter. Barlow also made a highlight defensive play in his opening stint, defending Avdija in isolation and rejecting his layup attempt. Bona then subbed in for Barlow with 3:23 left in the first quarter. He had a positive first possession, grabbing an offensive rebound and driving in for a dunk. Wade later played at center, too. Barlow logged 16 minutes and had six points. Bona recorded four points and two boards in five minutes. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse ended up using a 10-man rotation and did not play rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr. until fourth-quarter garbage time. Overall, the Sixers’ defense remained considerably worse without Embiid . The team also conceded 15 offensive rebounds, including five to Clingan. “I think your rim protection and ability to do that with some size is always a focal point of being really good defensively,” Nurse said. “And then you’ve got to do it a little bit by committee (with Embiid out). I thought, for the most part, I was looking at possessions where I liked our help into the paint. They were doing a good job of zinging it out. “I didn’t particularly like our (defense) back out. … There were a couple of times they missed those and still got rebounds. We were compacted in the lane with everybody because we didn’t get back out, and then still giving up an offensive rebound as well. That’s just playing through the possession, a little bit of energy, all that kind of stuff. … We just didn’t do enough pieces well.” Downward trend for Sixers’ defense Brown delivered tons of efficient offense for the Sixers in the first half and sure didn’t appear rusty. His layup late in the second quarter tied the game at 58-all. The five-time All-Star scored 19 first-half points on 8-for-10 shooting. Avdija exceeded Brown’s production, hitting heat-check threes, leaners through contact and just about everything he put up regardless of the defender. He tallied 25 points in the first half and shot 9 for 12 from the field. James reached 16 points when he capped a high-scoring half by nailing a corner three. The contest was even at 69 apiece heading into halftime. Monday’s game was James’ first of the season with three or more made three-pointers. The four-time MVP went 4 for 5 beyond the arc. He’d gone 10 for 46 (21.7 percent) over his first 13 games and was due for a good long-range night. James was whistled for his third foul early in the third quarter. Brown picked up his fourth with 10:15 to go in the period, forcing him to sit for an extended stretch. “I wasn’t too happy about it. … I think that affected the game,” Brown said. “It also affected my rhythm a little bit in the second half. I had to sit (almost) the whole third quarter. Coming back from injury, coming back from a hamstring thing, my body didn’t really feel the same after that.” Brown noted postgame that he had “a little bit of soreness and stuff like that.” “I think everything will check out,” he said. “The medical staff is on top of everything. Those hamstrings are tricky, so you want to make sure you play it the right way, be safe. I also don’t want to miss a lot of games, so I might be out there, but I’ve also got to be smart. I think I played it the right way today.” Avdija stopped lighting up the Sixers in the third period, but the team still had another unimpressive defensive quarter. Portland posted 32 points in the third and built its lead to double figures in the opening minute of the fourth. The game devolved into a blowout. An Avdija dunk put the Blazers’ advantage at 22 points with 5:15 on the clock and the Sixers didn’t have a miracle comeback in store. Even with all their wins, there’s no question the Sixers have been trending downward on defense over the past couple of weeks, allowing regular dribble penetration and plenty of comfortable threes. They’ll aim to raise their level on that side of the floor and expect Embiid’s presence to be a major help once he’s back in action. “I think it’s just mindset,” Walker said. “We’re capable when we want to. You need games like this every now and then just to remind you that it’s not as easy as it feels sometimes. It takes effort every game. “I think we can learn a lot from this. It’s just part of the growing pains, but I’m confident we’ll get back to that (early-season) level of defense. We have what it takes.”

stories.title: From Cooper Flagg to Ben Simmons, a look at Montverde Academy’s top NBA draft picks
stories.summary: From Cooper Flagg to Ben Simmons, here are the 10 highest NBA Draft picks to graduate from Montverde Academy in Florida.
stories.detailText: Montverde Academy (FL) has established itself as one of the premier pipelines for basketball talent in the country, producing NBA stars and some of the sport's most recognizable names. From No. 1 overall selections to first-round picks who have gone on to become franchise cornerstones, the Central Florida powerhouse has built an impressive résumé at the professional level. With three players selected first overall in the NBA Draft, here is a look at the 10 highest NBA Draft picks to graduate from Montverde Academy. Cooper Flagg, Dallas Mavericks (No. 1, 2025) The third Montverde Academy product to be selected No. 1 overall, Flagg was the centerpiece of the school's undefeated 2023-24 national championship team. After one season at Duke, he was selected first overall by Dallas in 2025 and won NBA Rookie of the Year in 2026. He is now emerging as the face of the Mavericks’ franchise Cade Cunningham, Detroit Pistons (No. 1, 2021) Cunningham became Montverde's second No. 1 overall selection after leading the Eagles alongside Scottie Barnes and Moses Moody. Following one season at Oklahoma State, he was drafted first overall by Detroit. He has since become a two-time NBA All-Star and led the Pistons' resurgence, including a 60-win season in 2025-26 Ben Simmons, Philadelphia 76ers (No. 1, 2016) Simmons became Montverde's first No. 1 overall NBA Draft pick after starring for the Eagles before playing one season at LSU. He won NBA Rookie of the Year in 2018 and became a three-time All-Star with Philadelphia and Brooklyn. His NBA career has since been derailed by injuries, and he is no longer an established NBA roster player. D'Angelo Russell, Los Angeles Lakers (No. 2, 2015) Russell helped lead Montverde to a national championship before playing one season at Ohio State. He was selected second overall by the Lakers and has gone on to play for several NBA franchises, including Brooklyn, Golden State, Minnesota and the Lakers. RJ Barrett, New York Knicks (No. 3, 2019) A former five-star recruit, Barrett starred at Montverde before playing one season at Duke. He was selected third overall by the Knicks and spent four-plus seasons in New York before being traded to Toronto in 2023. He remains a key member of the Raptors. Scottie Barnes, Toronto Raptors (No. 4, 2021) Barnes was part of Montverde's loaded 2020-21 team alongside Cunningham and Moody. After one season at Florida State, he was selected fourth overall by Toronto. He won NBA Rookie of the Year in 2022 and has since become a two-time All-Star and franchise cornerstone. Jalen Duren, Detroit Pistons (No. 13, 2022) Duren spent his final high school season at Montverde before playing one year at Memphis. Originally selected 13th overall by Charlotte, his draft rights were traded to Detroit. He has developed into one of the Pistons' key frontcourt players and earned his first NBA All-Star selection in 2026. Derik Queen, New Orleans Pelicans (No. 13, 2025) Queen was part of Montverde's undefeated 33-0 national championship team in 2023-24. Following one season at Maryland, he was selected 13th overall by Atlanta before being traded to New Orleans. He is now beginning his NBA career with the Pelicans. Moses Moody, Golden State Warriors (No. 14, 2021) Moody helped Montverde capture a national championship during the 2020-21 season before playing one year at Arkansas. He was selected 14th overall by Golden State and has developed into a rotation player for the Warriors. He is currently recovering from a ruptured patellar tendon suffered in March 2026. Precious Achiuwa, Miami Heat (No. 20, 2020) Achiuwa graduated from Montverde Academy in 2019 before playing one season at Memphis. He was selected 20th overall by the Miami Heat in the 2020 NBA Draft. He has since played for Miami, Toronto and the New York Knicks. For additional high school sports coverage, be sure to follow USA TODAY High School Sports on Instagram and X . stories.title: Knicks 121, Cavaliers 102: “The most Mike Brown victory imaginable”
stories.summary: Mike Brown and the Knicks find ways to secure their sixth straight victory.
stories.detailText: NEW YORK, NY - NOVEMBER 25: Jose Alvarado #5 of the New York Knicks drives to the basket during the game against the Cleveland Cavaliers as part of the 2026 Emirates NBA Cup on November 25, 2026 at Madison Square Garden in New York City, New York. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Nathaniel S. Butler/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images It’s easy to get lost in today’s world. Everything is spinning so fast, so many things are out of control. Prices, taxes, wars, narratives, diabolical devices, our sense of togetherness. Life sometimes feels like an endless list of things that, no matter how much you scratch off, no matter what you decide not to worry about, gets longer by the minute. The NBA is no exception, a cutthroat world infected by influencing influences that expects daily reinvention, that wants to turn humans into brands and expand like a kraken gobbling up the last little dollars from the deepest pits of the coral reef. As you watch another foul-baiting baller be rewarded for his deeds, followed by the 23rd commercial for guaranteed grifting, it can be tough to find the joy here from time to time, to remember why you ever thought this was fun. But then Jose Alvarado runs into the picture and steals a ball, only to rise up moments later for a three. He jumps for joy as he hits it, just like the little kid he once was on the playgrounds of the city that he now represents on the biggest stage there is in basketball. And you smile along with him. Jose Alvarado carries the Knicks to victory There is something inherently right about a guy like Jose Alvarado. Sure, he is an annoying pest defensively, loudmouthed, confident on his good days, cocky on his better ones. A guy you would probably hate if he wasn’t on your team. Not even in the fun way of hating an opponent, if there is one. No, you really can’t stand that little bugger, like, at all. Yet even if you root for some other franchise whose name doesn’t rhyme with clicks, deep down inside your basketball fan’s heart, you have to appreciate a guy, a man, a kid like Jose Alvarado. Mike Brown surely does. It didn’t even take Alvarado’s tide-turning performance in the Knicks’ 121-102 destruction of the Cleveland Cavaliers in yesterday’s NBA Cup game, which was, as PolyphonicSpreewell so beautifully put it in the Postgame Thread , “the most Mike Brown victory imaginable.” It didn’t take his 16 points in the fourth quarter or his 21 in total. But the light shining on Jose surely was a reminder that the big little Puerto Rican embodies what this New York basketball team is. Sure, they can beat you with Xs and Os, with the might of majestic superstars, with firepower that can put a New Year’s fireworks display to shame. But there is more that makes the Knicks the Knicks. A group that has a heart and a soul beyond what is expected of them, some inner power they can turn to when things go sideways. Something that lets them play and, more importantly, enjoy the game innocently, freely. How it was supposed to be experienced. JOSE ALVARADO TONIGHT 19 MINUTES 21 POINTS 3 ASSISTS 8-10 FG 5-7 3P +15 JOSEEEEEEEEE pic.twitter.com/NuCenpPTig — Teg🚨 (@IQfor3) November 26, 2026 Alvarado is not your type of guy? Pas de souci , says Pacôme Djenon Dadiet! It didn’t matter that he didn’t really hit shots consistently yesterday or, frankly, ever before. He still plunged into the action versus the James Hardens and Donovan Mitchells of the world like the Knicks’ bench was a cliff and his name was Orlando Duque. Maybe not as gracefully, but definitely just as committed and energetic. And, most importantly, without any fear. There was no fear in Tyler Nickel, either, who at some point seemed as far away from real NBA minutes as his birthplace in the Shenandoah Valley is from Madison Square Garden. But don’t worry, bench guy, Mike Brown’s got a map, and he knows where to find you. Mike Brown works his magic with the Knicks With injuries to OG Anunoby, Deuce McBride, and Jordan Clarkson, plus ineffective and almost shockingly bad nights from Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns, the coach seemingly didn’t have to search yesterday. He just hurled everyone he had on his pine into the action and watched them stick it to the Cavs. Mo Diawara hit a three. James Wiseman dominated the paint for stretches in the fourth quarter. He didn’t look out of place; he didn’t look like he didn’t know what he was doing. Rather, he played like a man possessed, not by some evil power or the One Ring to rule them all, but by the unwavering confidence and belief of a bald, happy-go-lucky man who coaches champions. These champions include a much-maligned Mikal Bridges, who carried the team throughout the entire second quarter. They also include Josh Hart and Landry Shamet, who did their thing and then some. They are all guys who had rough goes in the past but who never found themselves in Mr. Brown’s doghouse. They deserve to be singled out for pushing the ball in transition, for point-of-attack defense, for just being themselves. But frankly, who doesn’t? Everyone did a little and then a lot of what was needed from them. I’m sure Tyler Kolek was one of the biggest cheerleaders despite his rough night on the court. It all speaks to the culture that Mike Brown has bestowed upon this team, that he has created with all of his players. All of them. All these guys who know what hard work is. Who relish every opportunity they get. And who have a way of playing basketball that is as much fun as you can imagine.

stories.title: Clippers interim GM given full power to blow up roster at trade deadline

stories.detailText: Earlier this week, Marc Stein reported the Clippers are viewed as a “certain seller” with the NBA trade deadline approaching in February. Jack Fischer of The Stein Line said certain teams have expressed skepticism about what the Clippers might do. Fischer described the term “skepticism” as “misplaced” and said sources told him that interim general manager Trent Redden has been given the power to make “any moves he sees fit.” Brook Lopez playing in an NBA game for the Clippers against the Mavericks. NBAE via Getty Images Redden was the same member of the Clippers’ front office who finalized the decision to move Kawhi Leonard from Los Angeles to the Raptors over the offseason. According to Fischer, the Clippers have a few veteran pieces who could be dealt, including center Brook Lopez and wing Derrick Jones Jr. Fischer added the club wants to assess what its roster will look like with Brandon Ingram staying healthy. Ingram was acquired in the trade with Toronto for Leonard. He came over to Los Angeles with Gradey Dick, two first-round draft picks, including a first-round pick swap, and two second-round draft picks. Brandon Ingram making his season debut for the Clippers on Monday night against the Rockets. Getty Images Ingram missed the first month and a half of the season due to a partially torn Achilles tendon he suffered with the Raptors last season. He made his season debut on Monday. Ingram was the Clippers’ third-leading scorer in their 116-104 loss to Houston on Monday, but he gave the team a glimmering hope about his health. Ingram was on the court for 27 minutes and tallied 16 points, seven rebounds and four assists.

stories.title: Knicks assistant coach Chris Jent returns to team
stories.summary: Chris Jent was back on New York's bench for Wednesday night's NBA Cup win against Cleveland after a monthlong absence.
stories.detailText: NEW YORK -- Knicks assistant coach Chris Jent returned to the team Wednesday following a leave of absence . Jent stepped away from the Knicks in late October for an undisclosed reason, shortly after the season began. He was back on the bench for Wednesday night's 121-102 NBA Cup win against the Cleveland Cavaliers . Jent, 56, was a member of Knicks head coach Mike Brown's staff in Cleveland and was on the Charlotte Hornets ' coaching staff in 2024-25. He was the Orlando Magic 's interim coach for 18 games in 2004-05. Jent played at Ohio State from 1988 to 1992.

stories.title: 'All about giving': Why the Lakers' Ziaire Williams enjoys giving back
stories.summary: The sixth-year forward appreciates the little things in life and the ability to give back to the community as he did with a Thanksgiving event.
stories.detailText: Lakers forward Ziaire Williams celebrates after making a three-point shot during a win over the Jazz on Monday. (Ronaldo Bolanos / Los Angeles Times) As the gathering of kids began, their eyes grew wide and several of them said “oooh” when they saw the tall, slender young man with the stylish dreads approach the microphone and introduce himself as Lakers forward Ziaire Williams . Williams had come to Inglewood High to provide meals and fellowship with about 150 kids from the Boys & Girls Clubs of Metro Los Angeles , an event he has done for his entire six-year NBA career. Having grown up in Lancaster and attended Sierra Canyon, where he was a high school teammate of Bronny James, Williams saw himself in those kids. He, too, went to the Boys & Girls Club while a youth. He remembers the influence it made on his life and how his parents, Ziaire Williams Sr. and Marquita Fields-Williams, felt at ease because their son was safe. Williams, who held the event last week, believes it is important to be active in the community. “Being a part of a Thanksgiving event like this means a lot to me,” he told the kids. “I appreciate all of you guys coming out to support the event. This is a time of giving and Thanksgiving. It’s just all about giving back and being appreciative for your loved ones and all the small things in life. “So, I hope you guys can meet some new friends, eat some good food, and just appreciate the small things in life. That’s what it’s all about.” The kids cheered. Williams then helped to serve the food, a smile on his face, “joy” in his heart to see the kids enjoying the moment and each other, all of them relishing the opportunity to meet a Laker in person. “I’ve actually been doing this every year since I’ve been in the NBA,” Williams said. “Growing up, I was in the Boys & Girls Club. My parents were always at work. The Boys & Girls Club, it was almost like my second home growing up. It’s just a great safe place after school just to hang out, do your homework, meet some new friends and occasionally Christmas, Thanksgiving, hopefully have a good meal, maybe a pizza party or something. “So, since I’ve been in the NBA, I always try to just find different Boys & Girls Clubs I can partner with for just the holidays and seasons of giving. Now, just do my part to give back, give them something to smile about and, you can’t go wrong with a good meal.” Initially, some of the kids looked nervous and shy when they walked by Williams. But he greeted them all, shook hands, took pictures and listened to their stories. This was their day and Williams was happy to be a meaningful part of it. “Oh man, there’s no words like it, man. It’s hard to describe. It just makes my heart feel warm,” Williams said. “I feel like God gave me this amazing ability to play basketball, but he also has allowed me to use my talents to do events like this and give back. “And, man, it’s amazing. Every time I just get to hang out with kids and just see a smile on their face, it really just brings me back to when I was their age, and it’s amazing, man. There’s no words that can describe it.” Lakers forward Ziaire Williams dunks over Trail Blazers guard Scoot Henderson during a game earlier this month at Crypto.com Arena. (Gina Ferazzi / Los Angeles Times) By most accounts, the 6-foot-9 Williams, 25, is having his best season as a pro. He’s averaging 9.1 points per game and shooting career bests from the field (53.8%) and three-point range (42.1%). “Man, I would just say I just stuck with it. Just the same consistent work,” Williams said of his success. “Sometimes it doesn’t always pay off right away, but if you just keep sticking with it, keep being disciplined, your daily habits, it’s bound to change quick. As the late [rapper] Nipsey Hussle always says, just never quit. “Just the marathon always continues, and that’s a principle and a moral I live by, just continuing to always try to be the best version of myself every day. And I’m just grateful to be in this position. I’m on a great team, a winning team, guys who care about the game and guys who want to compete at the highest level. And it’s been an honor to play with the Lakers so far, and we still got a lot more work to do, but it’s been a great start for sure.” Whether starting or coming off the bench, Williams has delivered by being the quintessential three-and D player the Lakers expected. Before the Lakers signed Williams to a one-year, $3-million contract during free agency over the summer, they saw something else in him that made them yearn to have him as a member of their team. “He’s a beautiful human,” Lakers coach JJ Redick said. “I didn’t know him. We set up a workout for him in Vegas and he worked out. Rave reviews. I met with him the next day for about 45 minutes at our hotel and I was like, ‘I got to get this guy on my team. Regardless of the player, I got to get this person on my team.’ We sat there for 45 minutes and he looks you in the eye and it’s ‘yes sir, no sir. I got you, sir.’ He’s awesome. He’s an incredible human.” Lakers coach JJ Redick congratulates forward Ziaire Williams along the sideline as he comes off the court for a timeout. (Gina Ferazzi / Los Angeles Times) Both of Williams’ parents were in the military and he was taught to be respectful of others. So, what Redick saw and felt was real, because Williams was raised that way. “Yeah, it was definitely strict, but I’m thankful for it,” Williams said. “Just the discipline and just prioritizing certain things. It was never hard for me to do because I just grew up with that discipline always from Day 1. So, it was definitely hard. I got yelled at. I got my butt whipped a couple times. It was all for the greater good. My parents wanted me to just be the best young man I could possibly be and put myself in a better position than they were in.” He remembers going to LeBron James’ basketball camp in San Diego and winning the MVP award. That “was the coolest thing ever” to meet James. He remembers watching NBA games on TV and thinking how they “seemed like superheroes.” Now Williams is playing against James and those players he saw on TV. But when he does his basketball camps and his Thanksgiving events as he did last week, he doesn’t want the kids to view him as anything more than a humble person. “I don’t really want them to necessarily look at me as a superhero, but more so as just a person who’s always willing to give back,” Williams said. “I tie my shoes just the same way they do, you know? Every morning I just wake up and I thank God and I just try to be the best version of myself. “That’s what I just hope these kids get out of it is just whatever you put your mind to is possible. You just have to really believe in it and work at your craft every day. And I work on my craft every day and now it’s got me here with the Lakers.” Sign up for our weekly newsletter on all things Lakers. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

stories.title: Grading the Mavericks: Dallas’ accountability helped prevent a serious fall
stories.summary: The first step to fixing a problem is acknowledging that you have one
stories.detailText: The Mavericks went 4-2 over the last two weeks and sit at 11-7, in eighth place in the West. They lost back-to-back road games to Cleveland ( 127-117 ) and Boston ( 131-94 ), but rebounded with four straight wins against Golden State ( 116-94 ), the Clippers ( 110-100 ), Utah ( 116-114 ), and Denver ( 120-101 ). Cooper Flagg led the team in scoring with 23.7 points per game. Grade: B- The Mavericks did not start the last two weeks well. Losing back-to-back road games in embarrassing fashion, then giving a suboptimal performance against a really hurt Golden State team was pretty dire, despite the large margin of victory. The three games since have been pretty convincing; the Mavericks are a good team somewhere in the realm of “better than bad, not elite, but can win on any night”. We have seen the emergence, or more accurately, the rebirth of Caleb Martin in the last six games. He is scoring over 10 points per game, shooting 56.5 percent from three, and grabbing 2.3 steals per game over that stretch. Martin is the true definition of a glue guy and has held the team together in their four-game win streak. The win against Denver was incredible. It was an utterly dominant defensive performance. It is the type of win you have to build off of and refuse to let the train slow down. It was also Dallas’ third NBA Cup victory , meaning if they beat Phoenix on Friday, they will win their group. Straight A’s: Accountability Dallas’ two losses that applied to this round’s grades were part of a three-game skid that lacked effort in every sense of the word. Losing to a Cleveland team that sat all of their starters after travel issues was bad, but going into Boston the next day and losing the game in roughly six minutes (after Dallas went down 24-4) was a true wake-up call. Cooper Flagg said after the loss: “I don’t think we competed at a high enough level, you know, throughout the three games”. Every viewer noticed that, but having a guy in the fire acknowledge their shortcomings showed they could get through the adversity. And they did, to the tune of four straight wins. Even after the third victory in Utah, where they squandered a 17-point lead in three-and-a-half minutes, Kyrie Irving held the team, including the coaches, after practice to run in preparation for their game in Denver’s altitude. It paid off with a 19-point road victory. That is the sign of a good team. Being able to have honest conversations about your play and notice when things need to change is a key component of success. The Mavericks clearly have that. There will be more adversity and plenty more losses to come this season. If the Mavericks can lean on this framework, they will be solid, no matter what happens. Failed the assignment: Naji Marshall The Mavericks already have a weird roster, but the player that sticks out the most is Naji Marshall. He is not a good enough defender to justify the offensive dominance, and he turns the ball over far too much to be handling the ball at the rate he does. Part of his 20 percent usage rate is the fact that the roster is lacking ball handlers, but some of it, and perhaps the most frustrating part, is that he simply chooses to play hero ball far too often. It’s not clear when you look at his 10.9 points in 24.1 minutes per game. And sometimes he does play well enough to matter. But it’s the choice to keep a dribble handoff, or the pass that he forces in transition, or the insistence on taking floaters and shrinking the floor that really hurts the team. The extension Dallas signed him to already feels cumbersome, and I expect the best version of this team to not have him on the floor. Whether that is because he is benched or traded away, I am not sure. Extra Credit: Morez Johnson Jr. Maybe we have been spoiled by the likes of Luka Doncic and Cooper Flagg, or it’s the guys picked behind him playing well, but Johnson Jr., the ninth overall pick in this past draft, has felt overwhelmingly underwhelming. His athleticism does not jump off the screen a lot of the time, his offensive awareness is sketchy, and he fouls a bit too much to stay in the game consistently. That being said, he has shown flashes of being a really good glue piece to a great defensive team. One of these came against Dallas’ statement win in Denver, where he scored nine points and had a team-high 10 rebounds. He played excellent defense, had a monster dunk, moved his feet incredibly well, and impacted winning on all fronts. It is this type of game that makes you wonder why he can’t do this all the time. Some of it may be physical, with the shin splints still affecting him. A lot of it is probably mental. But either way, although the consistency isn’t there yet, you can see the vision finally.

stories.title: There’s something to like about the way the Suns lost in Houston
stories.summary: Rebounding remains a glaring weakness, while physicality and effort offer Phoenix a path toward sustained success.
stories.detailText: HOUSTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 25: Kevin Durant #7 of the Houston Rockets and Dillon Brooks #3 of the Phoenix Suns exchange words during the 2026 Emirates NBA Cup at Toyota Center on November 25, 2026 in Houston, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Phoenix Suns went to Space City to battle the team whose logo resembles one of those silly little patches that go on astronaut suits, ultimately losing by 12. What that final score doesn’t tell you is that with 4:45 remaining, the Suns were down three points. What killed them down the stretch is what killed them throughout the game, and it shouldn’t come as a surprise to any of us. Rebounding was the culprit. Or, more specifically, their inability to rebound. Phoenix was outrebounded 51-38 overall and 20-13 on the offensive glass, but it was the 27 second-chance points they surrendered that ultimately sunk them. When Alperen Sengun pulls down 11 rebounds, and seven of them are of the offensive variety, you know you’ve done something wrong. But my takeaway from this game? The impressively physical brand of basketball the Suns played. They stood up to a Rockets team that clearly had revenge on its mind as they ran up and down that bright red clowny court. After all, Phoenix had already beaten Houston earlier this season. When the Rockets came out with a chip on their shoulder, the Suns rose to the challenge and battled them throughout. The final result comes down to two things. Houston possesses a more talented roster, and they’re bigger, badder, and better on the boards. The attitude with which the Suns played, however, was something I thoroughly enjoyed watching. That’s who this team was a season ago, and perhaps they needed a team like Houston to push them around a little, to jostle them enough to draw a line in the sand and say, “We’re done with this.” The hope is that they carry that attitude forward. Because if they can bring that level of intensity and fight night in and night out, nobody is going to want to play that version of the Phoenix Suns. We know that because we saw it last year. The rebounding issues aren’t going away, and there will be nights when Phoenix simply doesn’t possess the personnel to overcome them. But physicality and effort are things this team can control regardless of the opponent. What we witnessed in Houston was a willingness to compete on somebody else’s terms without being intimidated by them. The Suns lost the basketball game, but somewhere on that obnoxiously red court, they rediscovered a little bit of their swagger. teamStories.detailText: Austin Reaves moved one step closer to making his return to the court on Thursday. The Lakers star was upgraded to questionable on the team’s injury report for Friday’s road game against the Spurs in San Antonio. Reaves was sidelined for the Lakers’ previous five games because of a bruised left heel injury he suffered during the third quarter of their Nov. 11 road win over the Bucks in Milwaukee. Austin Reaves (15) of the Los Angeles Lakers shoots a free throw. NBAE via Getty Images The team deemed his status day-to-day, but Thursday was the first time he was listed as questionable on one of the team’s injury reports since he’s been sidelined. The 6-foot-5 star guard was a full participant in the team’s practice on Wednesday. “It felt good to play basketball again,” Reaves said in his first public comments since suffering the injury. “Wind was a little bad, but kind of to be expected being out two weeks. But felt good.” Austin Reaves has been sidelined for five games because of his heel injury. NBAE via Getty Images He wasn’t sure what happened on the play against the Bucks to cause the injury. “I had no idea,” he said. “Tried to play through it, and then I drove baseline, planted on it, and was like, I can’t do this. So walked to the back and was in some pretty bad pain. I didn’t think I broke my foot, but it sure felt like I broke my foot.” The Lakers went 4-1 after Reaves suffered the injury, but the team clearly missed his offensive production. They had a 112.9 offensive rating (tied for No. 18) in the five games Reaves missed compared to the 121.6 (No. 1) offensive rating in their first 13 games. “Who would have thought that not having an elite offensive player, an All-Star level player would hurt your offense,” coach JJ Redick quipped. “That’s crazy.” Los Angeles Lakers’ Austin Reaves suffered his heel injury against the Bucks. AP Photo/Aaron Gash Reaves is averaging 24.7 points (51.3% shooting from the field, 40.9% on 3-pointers), 4.7 assists and 3.3 rebounds on the season. “One of those things that just, it sucks,” Reaves said. “I was rolling, playing well. We were rolling as a team, wanted to continue to be out there and play games. Hate missing games. But it’s one of those things, like I said, there wasn’t much that we could really do. But we took care of business.”

teamStories.title: What are Spurs fans thankful for this Thanksgiving?
teamStories.summary: It’s a good time to be a Spurs fan.
teamStories.detailText: SAN ANTONIO, TX - NOVEMBER 2: Victor Wembanyama #1 of the San Antonio Spurs smiles during the game against the Utah Jazz on November 2, 2026 at the Frost Bank Center in San Antonio, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photos by Michael Gonzales/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images The Spurs had a tough loss in Portland before the Thanksgiving break and will face arguably their biggest challenge yet when they face the West-leading Lakers after it. We are getting close to a quarter of the season being on the books, and games are starting to feel more meaningful as most teams round into shape. As the season progresses, it gets harder to sit back and just enjoy San Antonio basketball without any concerns, but fortunately Thanksgiving offers the perfect opportunity to think about all the good times it has provided already and to reflect on how lucky fans of the Silver and Black really are. Lee Dressie had a fantastic post about it that you should check out , but it would be interesting to see what you, the readers, are thankful for. Here’s my list, as a way to get things started. Victor Wembanyama This one is self-explanatory. Wembanyama is the most tantalizing talent to hit the league in a generation, and he’s a Spur. Luck got him to San Antonio, but he embraced the fanbase and seems to be happy to be in the city. He’s lived up to the hype and seems like a perfect fit for the franchise, adapting to its traditions and ways while staying eager to forge his own path. Watching Wemby is a joy for anyone who loves basketball, but it’s extra special to watch him dominate while wearing Silver and Black. Good health (compared to others) The Spurs will be without Dylan Harper due to a hip injury for a while longer. Fans have not even gotten to see how Tobias Harris looks on this team, as he’s been out since before preseason with a calf strain. A dirty play by Jeremiah Fears has forced De’Aaron Fox to sit out a few games. San Antonio has had its share of injuries. Fortunately, none of those injuries have sidelined anyone for the rest of the year and, if everything goes well (knocks frantically on wood), all three players should be back relatively soon. Other contenders have not been so lucky, so it’s important to be thankful for the injury luck the Spurs have had so far. A likable roster Sometimes fans are forced to root for players that, while talented, are not particularly likable. Whether because they are out of touch after becoming rich and famous or because of their personalities or bad behaviour, it can occasionally be hard to actually like the guys wearing the jersey. Luckily, that’s not a problem with the current Spurs. Sure, Wembanyama can come off as arrogant, but he also seems to have a good moral compass and is boring in a good way, putting basketball above everything. De’Aaron Fox always has a smile on his face and has adapted to any role asked of him. Harrison Barnes is the ultimate professional and a very charitable person. The young guards are hard workers who are willing to continue to improve instead of relying on talent and athleticism alone. Devin Vassell is soft-spoken but committed to winning, no matter what it takes. Even the guys who have struggled, like Keldon Johnson and Luke Kornet, have great personalities that make them lovable. It’s really hard to find someone to dislike on the roster, which makes watching the Spurs a lot more fun. No unsolvable problems This one is important to remember, especially after rough losses. The Spurs have fallen short in four games this season and have had some close calls against inferior opponents. It’s completely understandable to have some concerns about the team during the bad times, and occasionally even during the good times. The good news is, while there are some issues, none seem unsolvable. The Spurs have a ton of talent, so they can overcome some mistakes, which is great. The three-point shooting has been so bad that it’s bound to improve. The bench play has been poor, but it shouldn’t be impossible to find some lineups that work better. Having Harris back will certainly help the second unit. And if all else fails, a trade or a signing could give the team a boost if it needs one. San Antonio is in a great place already, but things could realistically get even better. Now let’s get to the important part. What are you thankful for as a Spurs fan? Let us know in the comments.

teamStories.detailText: The Lakers’ biggest test of the season is coming up. It’s not Friday, when they’ll face Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs. It’s Saturday, when the world will be reacting to whatever transpired. “Whether we lose the game, whether we win the game, we’re either going to be contenders on [ESPN’s] ‘First Take’ or we’re not going to be contenders and we’re fake,” Lakers coach JJ Redick said. “That stuff is just noise.” For the Lakers, their upcoming game against the Spurs is a temperature check. The teams are tied for the best record in the NBA at 15-3 . And their stars, Luka Doncic and Victor Wembanyama, are in a two-man race for the MVP Award. In other words, this is prime theater. And we all know what that means. San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama dunks against the Portland Trail Blazers in Portland, Ore., Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. AP Photo/Craig Mitchelldyer If the Lakers win, they’ll be the front-runners for the title . Doncic will officially be ahead of Wembanyama in the MVP race. The darlings of the NBA will be the crown jewel of the basketball world. But if they lose, well, the opposite will happen. There will be some version of sound the alarm. Press the panic button. The Lakers aren’t elite. Doncic isn’t the real deal. Walker Kessler can’t compete against the league’s top centers. So, the Lakers’ biggest test isn’t going to be whether they win a game in November. It’s going to be whether they can ignore the inevitable chatter when it becomes deafening. And it’s about to be dialed up to a feverish pitch. Luka Doncic (77) of the Los Angeles Lakers handles the ball against the Utah Jazz on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. NBAE via Getty Images That’s what happens when the two top teams in the league meet, especially when one of those teams is the Lakers, who are arguably under a more powerful magnifying glass than any other franchise in the league. It’s fun to talk about the Lakers. They’ve won 17 championships. They’ve had some of the biggest stars in NBA history, including Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Magic Johnson, Kobe Bryant, LeBron James and Doncic. They’re a globally recognized brand. When they win, they’re the talk of the town. When they lose, the sky is falling. They inspire overreactions. They’re the dream fodder for pundits. That’s where things get interesting. Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick watches his players during an NBA basketball game against the Utah Jazz in Los Angeles, Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. AP Photo/Kyusung Gong There are nine new players on the Lakers. They haven’t experienced the weight of that attention. It can be paralyzing. Even Doncic, who has been in the spotlight for most of his life , has never been the face of a franchise as big as the Lakers. This will be a major test. If the Lakers play great, they can’t let it get to their heads. And if they fall apart, they need to dust their shoulders and move forward. Championship teams lose games. But they don’t allow themselves to be defined by them. So, this game doesn’t matter and yet it means everything. It’s the ultimate test for a young group. And it has nothing to do with the score.

teamStories.detailText: PORTLAND, OR - November 25: Victor Wembanyama #1 of the San Antonio Spurs looks on during the game against the Portland Trail Blazers as part of the 2026 Emirates NBA Cup on November 25, 2026 at the Moda Center in Portland, Oregon. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Soobum Im/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images One of the few things I hope for as a spectator is that teams playing the late-night game bring it. It’s too hard to stay awake as it is after a long day, so fans need excitement to keep them from falling asleep. Fortunately, it was not a problem for these teams, yet the only issue the San Antonio Spurs had late was their basketball IQ. I had this game circled on the calendar because the physicality was off the charts the last time they played on Nov. 7. It appears it was not a distant memory for the Portland Trail Blazers, as the ESPN broadcast highlighted how they felt embarrassed by that game and wanted their lick back. Nonetheless, it was grown-up hoops and it wouldn’t be a surprise if these squads didn’t like each other. Wednesday night being an Emirates Cup game added to the fun because the winner would keep their hopes alive of getting to the quarterfinal, still needing to get by Friday’s game. Keep in mind that getting to the next round guarantees the players $60,499 and half of that for the two-way guys. I wish that coach Mitch Johnson hadn’t stuck to his usual substitution patterns in the third quarter, because when Wembanyama sat the Spurs were instantly outscored by eight. They got back on track when Victor checked in to clean up the mess, and the team likely could have separated itself had he had a longer shift. Games like this with absences to key guys magnify every decision. While the most part Mitch was good, I shook my head as he tried to buy time for the starters with Carter Bryant and Ja’Kobi Gillespie at the start of the fourth. Johnson was probably thinking about preserving his main guys for later games, but this wasn’t this a big one? Every now and then, 40 minutes against good teams is not so bad, and he probably would have broken 50 points for the third time this year. Aside from their cup chances, the three late turnovers and failure to stop Portland’s two 3-pointers ruined Wemby’s 44-point masterpiece. Of course, the Trail Blazers deserve credit, but the Spurs also beat themselves down the stretch. Stephon Castle’s eight-second violation was a killer. Props to coach Micah Nori. He has a serious team, while he’s basically on a prove-it deal, and they’ve been without Ja Morant. A lot of it has to do with them having one of the most balanced teams in the league, and it helps that Damian Lillard is still one sport’a clutch shooters. He has come back from his Achilles tear with his first step intact, and his outburst in the second half was vintage. Takeaways: Without De’Aaron Fox and Dylan Harper, the Spurs were without two of the league’s best penetrators (sorely needed against a high-level defense) which is a big reason why Wemby was the only one to score more than six points in the lane. The Spurs only had two quarters in which the offense was running smoothly (posting a 112.1 offensive rating) and that is one of their four-worst showings of the season. Portland was able to slow them down by making them pass less often. Wembanyama stepped up. He poured in jumpers as Portland got physical with him. He kept the pressure on Donovan Clingan and fouled him out with four minutes left. In the past, Wembanyama wouldn’t always assert himself in those situations and now it’s like radar is beeping when his man gets five personals. The Spurs mostly get the shot they are looking for when running the horns set, which has a screen to the left and right for the ball handler. The team has the best results on these when the screener is the scorer and the ball handler is the decoy. Bryant should model his game after Keldon Johnson’s. The latter barely scored but has mastered the art of hustle and had 12 rebounds, including five offensive, on Wednesday. Portland is arguably the best paint-attacking team in the league, averaging 61.7 drives per game, and Deni Avdija has a lot to do with that. Wembanyama had 12 points in the third quarter when he was subbed out and had only logged 21 total minutes to that point. As his rampage was paused, I was reminded of the old joke about how the only person who could stop Michael Jordan was Dean Smith.

teamStories.detailText: Which two teams will face off inside Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis for the 2026 Emirates NBA Cup championship? There's just one more night of games until the quarterfinal bracket is unveiled. Over the summer, the league unveiled the full group stage schedule for the in-season tournament, with action taking place every Friday from Oct. 30 to Nov. 27 and on special Cup nights during Thanksgiving week (Nov. 24-25). After the New York Knicks became the first team to win the NBA Cup and Finals in the same season, can Jalen Brunson & Co. keep their championship run going? They'll have plenty of competition, specifically within the star-studded East Group B. Here's what you need to know about the in-season tournament, now in its fourth year. Jump to a section: Schedule | Groups | FAQ Takeaways Trail Blazers 116, Spurs 111 The Portland Trail Blazers survived a 44-point, 16-rebound effort from Victor Wembanyama for a dramatic home win over the San Antonio Spurs on Wednesday, plunging the West Group C standings into chaos and setting up a pair of do-or-die NBA Cup opening-round finales. Blazers star Deni Avdija collected a pass from Damian Lillard and banked in a clutch 3-pointer from the top of the key with 37.9 seconds left to stun the Spurs, who entered Wednesday tied for the West's best record. Avdija posted a team-high 32 points to go with 11 rebounds and seven assists, and Lillard added 29 points and six assists. Wembanyama, carrying San Antonio without injured teammates De'Aaron Fox , Dylan Harper and Tobias Harris , notched his fifth 40-point effort of the season. But the Spurs, who reached the Cup final last season, still have work to do to advance to the tournament's eight-team knockout round. With the win, Portland created a four-way tie atop West Group C. The Spurs, Blazers, Golden State Warriors and Los Angeles Lakers all have identical 2-1 records in group play, while the Sacramento Kings have been eliminated from the tournament with an 0-4 mark. The Spurs will host the Lakers on Friday in a highly anticipated showdown between West powerhouses. On the same night, the Blazers will host the Warriors. Per the Cup format, the winner of each group automatically advances to the knockout stage and the second-place teams vie for a wild-card spot. San Antonio will finish first in Group C with a win over the Lakers and a Blazers loss. Portland will finish first with a win over Golden State and a San Antonio win. Los Angeles will finish first with a win over San Antonio and a Portland win. Golden State will finish first with a win over Portland and a San Antonio win. The two West Group C teams that lose Friday will be eliminated. Timberwolves 113, Thunder 106 The Minnesota Timberwolves scored a key road win over the Oklahoma City Thunder on Wednesday to maintain control of their NBA Cup destiny, but they lost star guard LaMelo Ball to an ankle injury in the closing minutes. Jaden McDaniels and Ball helped the Timberwolves to improve to 3-0 in West Group B play by outlasting back-to-back MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander at Paycom Center. McDaniels finished with a team-high 32 points to go with 10 rebounds and five assists, and Ball added 19 points, seven rebounds and eight assists. With 2:29 left in regulation and Minnesota clinging to a 105-104 lead, Ball landed on Thunder center Isaiah Hartenstein 's foot in a scramble for a contested rebound. The All-Star guard, who was acquired by Minnesota from the Charlotte Hornets in an offseason trade, had to be helped off the court and did not return. Nevertheless, the Timberwolves closed out the win with an 8-2 run thanks to guard Ayo Dosunmu , who made a layup and a clutch 3-pointer to ice the win. Minnesota can advance to the eight-team knockout round of the Cup by beating the Memphis Grizzlies (2-1 in group play) on Friday. Even if the Timberwolves lose that game, they are still well-positioned to advance to the knockout round as a wild card thanks to their plus-39 point differential. Oklahoma City (2-2) is now at serious risk of being eliminated in the Cup's group stage for the first time since 2023. The Thunder reached the 2024 Cup final and advanced to the semifinals last season. Gilgeous-Alexander, who is carrying an injury-ravaged roster, posted 32 points and five against Minnesota. The LA Clippers (1-2) are long shots to advance from West Group B, and the New Orleans Pelicans (0-3) have already been eliminated. -- Ben Golliver 76ers 111, Heat 104 The Miami Heat 's seven-game winning streak is over, but their NBA Cup hopes are still very much alive. Tyrese Maxey and LeBron James led the Philadelphia 76ers to a home victory over the Heat on Wednesday to deal Miami its first loss in Cup play and claim the top spot in East Group B. Maxey led Philadelphia with a team-high 30 points, and James posted 25 points, 10 rebounds and 12 assists to register his first triple-double since signing with the 76ers during the offseason. Thanks to their win and the Cleveland Cavaliers ' loss to the New York Knicks on Wednesday, the 76ers now control their own destiny. If Philadelphia (2-1 in group play) beats the Indiana Pacers in their Cup finale on Friday, it will automatically advance to the tournament's eight-team knockout round because the 76ers would finish atop the group. They hold a head-to-head tiebreaker against the Heat (2-1 in group play) thanks to Wednesday's victory. Even if the 76ers win Friday, the Heat can still finish second in the group and claim a wild card spot. After managing to cut a 16-point Philadelphia lead to a seven-point loss, Miami holds a healthy plus-25 point differential heading into their cup finale against New York on Friday. The Cavaliers (2-2 in group play), Pacers (1-2) and Knicks (1-2) haven't yet been eliminated from advancing to the knockout round, though they face more difficult paths than the 76ers or Heat. The pre-Thanksgiving showdown between Philadelphia and Miami pitted James against Giannis Antetokounmpo in a matchup of NBA Cup MVPs. James led the Los Angeles Lakers to the inaugural Cup championship in 2023, and Antetokounmpo led the Milwaukee Bucks to the 2024 Cup crown. Antetokounmpo led the Heat with 32 points and 14 rebounds in a losing effort. The 76ers improved to an East-leading 15-4 record by beating the Heat despite losing forward Jaylen Brown to hamstring tightness before halftime. Brown departed with six points in 17 minutes. format? NBA commissioner Adam Silver has had a longstanding fascination with European soccer. Establishing an in-season cup competition within the NBA schedule came from soccer leagues having both a regular-season title, won by the team with the most points over the full year, and a separate tournament (or, in some leagues, multiple tournaments) that runs concurrently with the league season. In England, for example, there are the various divisions -- led by the Premier League -- and also the FA Cup competition. But unlike those European leagues, which play their cup competitions outside of their league schedules, the NBA Cup is built in to the regular-season slate. The 30 NBA teams are split into six five-team groups -- three featuring Eastern Conference teams and three comprising Western Conference teams -- with each team then playing one game against the other four in its group. The winner of each group, plus the team with the best record among the non-group winners, advances to the knockout stage of the competition. How will this impact the regular-season schedule and standings? Typically, the NBA sends out a full 82-game schedule in mid-August. Now, the league sends out only 80 games and leaves a gap of roughly a week to fill in later, depending on how the group stage of the NBA Cup plays out. The two teams from the East and West that lose in the quarterfinals will play their 82nd game against each other. Meanwhile, the 22 teams that fail to qualify for the knockout rounds will have their final two games scheduled -- one at home and one on the road against others eliminated in the group stage. The teams that reach the NBA Cup final will actually play 83 games -- though the championship game won't count toward the standings or any statistical markers. The four teams that reach the semifinals will have completed their 82 games and won't need any other games added to their schedule. Any team that makes it to the semifinals will have that game moved later in the schedule to avoid back-to-back games. The NBA made this change in an effort to avoid having empty days on the calendar while attempting to minimize back-to-backs for all teams as much as possible. Where are the semifinals and final being played? In a shift from previous tournaments, the quarterfinals and semifinals will be played at home sites. The Dec. 11 title game, meanwhile, will move from Las Vegas to the storied Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis. NBA commissioner Adam Silver previously said the league was searching for "storied college arenas" to play host to the Cup final. (No venue has been announced for 2027.) Why does the NBA Cup include regular-season games? Before its launch, one of the main questions surrounding the in-season tournament was why any team would be incentivized to compete in it. The NBA ensured teams will be motivated by making every game part of the season and, as in-conference matchups, potentially important to playoff tiebreakers. If this had been set up like the cup tournaments in European soccer, there would have been nothing stopping NBA teams from opting out by sitting their top players for extra rest. Which teams make up the groups? To create the groups, the NBA put the 15 teams in each conference into five pots, separated by their finish last season. Pot 1 included the teams that finished in the top three in the regular-season standings, Nos. 4-6 in the standings went into Pot 2, Nos. 7-9 into Pot 3, Nos. 10-12 into Pot 4 and Nos. 13-15 into Pot 5. As a result, the following groups were drawn: East Group A Detroit Pistons Toronto Raptors Orlando Magic Milwaukee Bucks Brooklyn Nets East Group B New York Knicks Cleveland Cavaliers Philadelphia 76ers Miami Heat Indiana Pacers East Group C Boston Celtics Atlanta Hawks Charlotte Hornets Chicago Bulls Washington Wizards West Group A Denver Nuggets Houston Rockets Phoenix Suns Dallas Mavericks Utah Jazz West Group B Oklahoma City Thunder Minnesota Timberwolves LA Clippers New Orleans Pelicans Memphis Grizzlies West Group C San Antonio Spurs Los Angeles Lakers Portland Trail Blazers Golden State Warriors Sacramento Kings Does one group stand out the most from the others? East Group B is a monster. All five teams -- defending NBA Cup and Finals champion New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland, Miami and Indiana -- are among the favorites to win the conference in 2026-27. The group stage will also feature reunion games for LeBron James , when the 76ers face the Cavs and Heat. And after guard Tyrese Haliburton missed the entire 2025-26 season while rehabbing a torn Achilles, the Pacers will be back among the East elite and hungry to reach the title game in Indianapolis. What do players get for winning? In 2023, the first year the tournament was held, the players on the winning team received $500,000 each and the runners-up got $200,000. The losing players of the semifinals each got $100,000, and those ousted in the quarterfinals got $50,000. Now, in each subsequent year, the prizes will be slightly higher, as a result of negotiated raises year over year to keep pace with increases in the salary cap and basketball-related income as part of the most recent collective bargaining agreement between the NBA and the National Basketball Players Association. Will anyone earn individual honors for their play in NBA Cup games? There will be an MVP award, as well as an all-tournament team. Will this have any impact on the playoffs? Not beyond the games counting in the regular-season standings (and toward tiebreakers). The only playoff impact comes from the wins and losses accrued throughout the tournament. Though there was debate among league insiders about guaranteeing a playoff berth for winning the tournament, ultimately that idea (or any other to further incentivize teams) was not enacted. Why is it called the Emirates NBA Cup? The league struck a sponsorship deal with Emirates, the Dubai-based airline, to sponsor the tournament after its initial run. The NBA said last year that it went with the most basic titles for both the tournament and its trophy -- the "in-season tournament" and "NBA Cup" -- as a way to introduce the concept to fans. However, using such nondescript names had another clear advantage: It gave the league a blank slate in case it sold the naming rights for the tournament and cup to a sponsor and avoided the complications that could arise by naming them after someone (for example, late NBA commissioner David Stern, one possibility that had been floated before the tournament was officially unveiled). After Thursday's 39-38 loss to the Eagles, Cowboys owner and G.M. Jerry Jones was asked about McCarthy, who coached Jones's team for five seasons, from 2020 through 2024. "I offered him to stay at least another year when he left," Jones told reporters. "And so I thought he was outstanding as the head coach and had a great command of, frankly, quarterback, offense. Can't say enough good things about him. He's, frankly, one of the finest people that around football that I've been around. And I can't say enough about him.
